Advisory Opinion No. 25-03: Applying the State ethics laws and
regulations to a legal defense fund
INTRODUCTION
It has been widely reported that Attorney General Letitia James is accepting
contributions submitted through the Democratic Attorneys General Association (DAGA) to
defray some or all of her legal defense expenses in connection with the federal criminal
prosecution of the Attorney General in the United States District Court for the Eastern District
of Virginia. The Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government (“Commission”) has
received inquiries from the public asking whether this arrangement complies with State ethics
laws and, if so, how. The Commission issues this formal Advisory Opinion to explain how and
why the Attorney General may receive legal defense contributions from DAGA consistent with
the requirements of New York’s ethics laws and the Commission’s regulations and existing
advisory opinions.
APPLICABLE LAW
Section 73(5)(a) of the Public Officers Law (POL) prohibits a State officer or employee
from directly or indirectly soliciting, accepting, or receiving any gift where the circumstances
reasonably permit an inference that the gift was intended or could be expected to influence the
official, or was intended as a reward for official action on the State official’s part.1
POL § 73(5)(b) prohibits State officials2 from soliciting, accepting, or receiving any gift
from a registered lobbyist or client, unless under the circumstances it is not reasonable to infer
that the gift was intended to influence the State official.3
1 Public Officers Law § 73(5)(a).
2 Hereinafter, “State official” shall refer to all State officers and employees including the four statewide elected
officials, members and employees of the legislature, and heads of State agencies.
3 Public Officers Law § 73(5)(b).

POL § 73(5)(c) prohibits State officials from permitting the solicitation, acceptance, or
receipt of any gift from a registered lobbyist or client to a third party, including a charitable
organization, under circumstances that reasonably permit an inference that the gift was
intended or could be expected to influence the official.4
The Commission’s gift regulations for State officials, set forth at Title 19 NYCRR Part 933,
utilize the concept of an “Interested Source” to identify gifts that are offered or accepted under
presumptively prohibited circumstances. Interested Sources include lobbyists and their clients,5
and any other party that does or seeks to do business with the public official or the official’s
agency or has some other private interest in influencing the public official.6 A gift from an
Interested Source is presumptively impermissible unless all three of the following criteria are
satisfied:
(1) it is not reasonable to infer that the Gift was intended to influence the public
official; and
(2) the Gift could not reasonably be expected to influence the public official in
the performance of his or her official duties; and
4 Public Officers Law § 73(5)(c).
5 All lobbyists and their clients, who are in the business of influencing government decision-making, are
presumptively prohibited from offering or giving a gift to any public official regardless of whether they have
specific interests pending before the official or the official’s agency. However, this presumption is rebuttable based
on an examination of the circumstances surrounding the gift. A lack of a particularized interested before the public
official or their agency will tend to rebut the presumption. DAGA is not a registered lobbyist or the client of a
lobbyist in New York.
6 The term “Interested Source” is defined at 19 NYCRR Part 933.2(l):
(l) Interested Source shall mean any person or entity who on his or her own behalf, or on behalf of an
entity, satisfies any one of the following: (1) is regulated by, negotiates with, appears before in other
than a Ministerial Matter, seeks to contract with or has contracts with, or does other business with: (i)
the Legislative Member, the Legislative Employee, or the State Officer or Employee, in his or her official
capacity; (ii) the State Agency with which the State Officer or Employee is employed or affiliated; or (iii)
any other State Agency when the State Officer or Employee’s agency is to receive the benefits of the
contract; or (2) with respect to a Legislative Member or a Legislative Employee, is required to be listed
on a statement of registration pursuant to § 1-e(a)(1) of article 1-A of the Legislative Law, or is the
spouse or unemancipated child of any person required to be listed on a statement of registration
pursuant to § 1-e(a)(1) of article 1-A of the Legislative Law; or (3) with respect to State Officers and
Employees, is required to be listed on a statement of registration pursuant to § 1-e(a)(1) of article 1-A of
the Legislative Law and lobbies or attempts to influence actions, decisions, or policies of the State
Agency with which the State Officer or Employee is employed or affiliated; or (4) with respect to State
Officers and Employees, is the spouse or unemancipated child of any individual satisfying the
requirements of section 933.2(l)(3); or (5) is involved in any action or proceeding, in which
administrative and judicial remedies thereto have not been exhausted, and which is adverse to either:
(i) the State Officer or Employee in his or her official capacity; or (ii) the State Agency with which the
State Officer or Employee is employed or affiliated; or (6) has received or applied for funds from the
State Agency with which the Covered Person is employed or affiliated at any time during the previous 12
months up to and including the date of the proposed or actual receipt of the item or service of more
than Nominal Value.
2

(3) it is not reasonable to infer that the Gift was intended as a reward for any
official action on the public official’s part.7
A non-Interested Source is a person or entity that has no particularized interest in
influencing the public official. A gift from a non-Interested Source is presumptively permissible
unless one or more of the following three criteria is met:
(1) it could reasonably be inferred that the Gift was offered or given with the
intent to influence the Covered Person, or
(2) the Gift could reasonably be expected to influence the Covered Person in the
performance of his or her official duties, or
(3) it could reasonably be inferred that the Gift was offered or given with the
intent to reward the Covered Person for any official action on his or her part.8
In Advisory Opinion No. 20-02, the Joint Commission on Public Ethics discussed how to
analyze a gift given to a third party at the direction or request of a State official. Factors to
consider in analyzing the circumstances surrounding such a gift include the nature of the
solicitation, if any; the substance of any communication involving the State official; the nature
and purpose of the gift; the nature and purpose of the third-party recipient; the extent of the
public official’s knowledge regarding the gift; the nature of any official business involving the
donor that is pending before the State official; any nexus between the solicitation and the
pending business; and the offeror’s history of making similar gifts.
It is noted that the New York Election Law permits a State official to use campaign funds
to pay legal defense costs,9 but campaign contributions are excluded from the definition of
“gift” under the gift regulations, and therefore are not subject to Interested Source analysis.10
However, this Advisory Opinion addresses contributions of funds specifically to defray legal
defense costs, which would constitute gifts under the regulations, and therefore must satisfy
the Interested Source test.
DISCUSSION
The Commission staff has relied on public reporting and private inquiries to develop an
insider’s understanding of DAGA’s defense fund operations. Staff determined that DAGA is not
an Interested Source with respect to the Office of the Attorney General (OAG). The mere fact
that DAGA supports the Attorney General politically does not make DAGA an Interested Source
under the gift regulations. DAGA has no particularized interest in any specific matter pending
before the Attorney General, so the Attorney General can't take an official action intended to
7 19 NYCRR Part 933.3(a)
8 15 19 NYCRR Part 933.3(b).
9 See Election Law § 14-130.
10 See Title 19 NYCRR Part 933.4(a)(4), which excludes political campaign contributions from the definition of “gift.”
3

directly benefit DAGA. Therefore, DAGA’s contributions to the Attorney General’s legal defense
are presumptively permissible.
The next question is whether the underlying contributions to DAGA constitute
prohibited third-party gifts to the Attorney General. An examination of the facts indicates they
do not.
DAGA operates as a political organization under Section 527 of the Internal Revenue
Code. The identities of donors to DAGA as a Section 527 political organization are not required
to be, and will not be, publicly reported. DAGA has an affiliate, the Progressive State Leaders
Committee (PSLC), which operates as an advocacy organization under Section 501(c)(4).
Contributions to the Section 501(c)(4) organization, even if directed to a specific fund, are
reported only as contributions to the organization. Therefore, no individual defense fund
contributors will be publicly identified.
Commission staff has been informed that DAGA has established a three-member
allocation committee to independently review requests for legal defense funding and allocate
available funds. The Attorney General does not have a representative on this committee. The
OAG has vetted the committee members and has imposed a requirement that it be informed
when and if any member of the committee is replaced so that the OAG can vet the new
member.
The Commission is satisfied that under the described protocol, contributions to the legal
defense fund do not constitute prohibited third-party gifts to the Attorney General. The
Attorney General would only know – at most – that the contributions came from the
organization. Since there would be, effectively, no identifiable underlying donor, and given that
the organization itself has no specific interests pending before the OAG and is not an Interested
Source, there will be no reasonable basis to infer that any contribution was given with the
intent to influence the Attorney General, or that the contribution could be expected to
influence the Attorney General, or that the contribution was given with the intent to reward
the Attorney General, for any official action on her part
If the Attorney General comes to learn the identity of an Interested Source donor who
made the donation with the intent that it be used in whole or in part to pay for her legal
defense, the Attorney General would be obligated to recuse herself from any matter before the
OAG involving the donor and return the donation on a pro-rata basis.
To avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, the Commission cautions that the
Attorney General should not attend any event held for the benefit of DAGA, in whole or in part.
because such an event could appear to be a de facto fundraising event for the Attorney
General. The Attorney General cannot personally solicit (or direct campaign staff, governmental
staff, or anyone else to solicit) legal defense contributions through DAGA from any Interested
Source. On her annual statement of financial disclosure for the applicable reporting period, the
Attorney General will be required to disclose DAGA’s contributions to her legal defense in
4

response to Question 9, and the Attorney General’s interest in DAGA’s defense fund must be
disclosed in response to Question 11.
CONCLUSION
The Commission concludes that the Attorney General can accept legal defense funds
under the proposed arrangement with DAGA, consistent with this Advisory Opinion. The OAG
must contact the Commission if it learns that any of the information contained herein is
inaccurate or if there will be or has been a material change in the processes surrounding
DAGA’s legal defense fund.
5

Advisory Opinion No. 25-02: Finding that compliance with Public
Officers Law Section 73(8-b) satisfies the
requirements in Public Officers Law Section
73(4)(a) with respect to a former employee
of the certifying agency who is currently
employed by another State agency
INTRODUCTION
The following advisory opinion is issued by the New York State Commission on Ethics
and Lobbying in Government (“Commission”), pursuant to Executive Law § 94(7)(c). On
December 11, 2024, staff received a submission from [a state agency] seeking leave pursuant to
Public Officers Law § 73(8-b) to contract with a recently retired agency employee, [ ], to
render services to [the agency] notwithstanding that the post-employment provisions in the
Public Officers Law prohibited [the former employee] from contracting with or otherwise
providing services to her former employing agency. This request was presented to the
Commission at its meeting on December 18, 2024, and was approved. In line with the request,
Commission staff informed [the state agency] that it could contract with [the former employee]
for a term not to exceed six months, at an hourly rate of $58.00 and a maximum payment of
$13,920.
Unbeknownst to Commission staff, after leaving [the agency]’s employ, [the former
employee] had accepted employment with [another state agency]. This fact became known to
staff on February 21, 2025, when staff received a request from [the former employee], now as an
[employee of the second agency], with [the second agency]’s approval, for approval of an
outside activity, i.e., approval to render contractual services to [first agency] as an outside
activity. According to information subsequently obtained from [first agency]’s ethics officer, [the
former employee] started her job with the [second agency] on December 16, 2024. Thus, when
the Commission approved the 8-b application, [the former employee] was a State employee
again.
This raised the question of whether Public Officers Law § 73(4)(a) applied to [the former
employee] when she entered into the contract with [the first agency]. Section 73(4)(a) provides,
in pertinent part, that no State officer or employee can contract to provide goods or services to
any State agency unless the contract is let after public notice and competitive bidding. Since [the

former employee] was a State employee when she entered into the contract with [the first
agency], there were questions as to whether Section 73(4)(a) invalidated the contract and
whether Section 73(8-b) is available when the former agency employee is currently employed
elsewhere in State government. The Commission hereby concludes that in the situation
presented, Section 73(8-b) applies notwithstanding that the certifying agency’s employee is
currently employed by another state agency and both satisfies and outweighs the provisions of
Section 73(4)(a). [The former employee] may render contractual services to [the first agency] as
an outside activity with respect to her regular employment with [the second agency], and HCR
need not engage in public notice and competitive bidding for those services.
APPLICABLE LAW
Public Officers Law § 73(4)(a) prohibits a State officer or employee from entering into a
contract with any State agency absent public notice and a competitive bidding process:
[N]o statewide elected official, state officer or employee, member of the legislature,
legislative employee or political party chairman or firm or association of which such
person is a member, or corporation, ten per centum or more of the stock of which is
owned or controlled directly or indirectly by such person, shall (i) sell any goods or
services having a value in excess of twenty-five dollars to any state agency, or (ii)
contract for or provide such goods or services with or to any private entity where the
power to contract, appoint or retain on behalf of such private entity is exercised, directly
or indirectly, by a state agency or officer thereof, unless such goods or services are
provided pursuant to an award or contract let after public notice and competitive bidding.
On its face, this provision appears to apply to the contract between [the first agency] and
[its former employee], since [the former employee] was a State employee working with the
[second agency] when she entered into the contract, which was valued at over $25.
However, Public Officers Law § 73(8-b) permits a State agency to seek leave to contract
with a former employee who is otherwise prohibited by the post-employment restrictions from
entering into an employment contract with their former agency. Section 73(8-b) states in relevant
part:
Notwithstanding the provisions of subparagraphs (i) and (ii) of paragraph (a) of
subdivision eight of this section, a former state officer or employee may contract
individually, or as a member or employee of a firm, corporation or association, to render
services to any state agency if, prior to engaging in such service, the agency head certifies
in writing to the commission on ethics and lobbying in government that such former
officer or employee has expertise, knowledge or experience with respect to a particular
matter which meets the needs of the agency and is otherwise unavailable at a comparable
cost. . . . The commission on ethics and lobbying in government must review and approve
all certifications made pursuant to this subdivision.
2

DISCUSSION
Section 73(4)(a), which applies to current State employees, is an important provision that
balances the state’s need to acquire necessary goods and services for the lowest cost against the
need to prevent the appearance of a conflict of interest when a State officer or employee seeks to
do business with the state. By requiring that such business be conducted only pursuant to an open
and competitive bidding process, the State can obtain necessary goods and services, while the
competitive bidding requirement helps to ensure that the best bid wins the contract. Based on a
plain reading of the statute, permitting [the employee], an active State employee, to enter into a
no-bid contract with [the first agency] can be seen as violating the letter and spirit of Section
73(4)(a).
However, despite re-joining the State workforce with the [the second agency] after
leaving [the first agency]’s employ, [the employee] was still subject to the two-year bar set forth
in Public Officers Law § 73(a)(i) as a former employee [of the first agency].1 (The government-
to-government exception to the post-employment restrictions – set forth at Section 73(8)(e) –
does not apply to [the employee]’s situation because she is not working for [the first agency] in
her capacity as an employee [of the second agency].) The two-year bar’s prohibition on
appearing and practicing before one’s former agency prevented [the employee] from entering
into a contract with [the first agency] or preparing specific material in response to any matter
before [the first agency during that two-year period.2
The fact that [the employee] was employed by the [second agency] did not change the
calculus for [the first agency] in any way. [The employee] was still a former employee [of the
first agency] who was prohibited from contracting with [that agency], while [that agency] still
had a need that could only be filled at reasonable cost by contracting with [its former employee].
Section 73(8-b) was intended by the legislature to alleviate exactly this tension. The sponsor’s
memorandum accompanying the proposed bill reflects that this Commission’s predecessor
agency, the State Ethics Commission, supported the proposal:
[T]he commission understands that the post-employment restrictions have, in some
instances, worked to the detriment of the state by precluding an agency from retaining the
services of a former state employee where the former employee has special expertise and
could perform the services in a more cost-effective manner. . . . This proposal recognizes
the state's interest in obtaining expertise at reasonable cost in such situations.3
The State Ethics Commission further noted that the post-employment restrictions made
[n]o distinction between the former employee's working in the interest of the state and
against its interests. This bill would allow such a differentiation in some cases. By linking
the exception to a particular matter, requiring agency head certification and review and
approval by the commission, this bill includes sufficient safeguards that will allow the
1 See Advisory Opinion 95-19 (holding that when a State employee leaves one agency and joins another, the two-
year bar is measured from the dates the former employee left each agency). Thus, [the former employee]’s two-year
bar with respect to [the first agency] began to run on the date she left [that agency].
2 Advisory Opinion 90-04.
3 Sponsor’s memorandum, L.2004 ch. 523.
3

state to obtain needed expertise while preventing agencies from providing a "golden
parachute" to an employee who leaves his or her position.4
Notably, nothing in the history of the provision or in its rationale suggests that the
reference to “former state officer or employee” in Section 73(8-b) was intended to preclude its
application to former agency employees who had subsequently become employed by a different
state agency. Assuming, as here, that the currently employing agency also approved the
arrangement or had no objection to it, which is the prerogative of any agency, there would be no
reason to deprive the former agency of the limited but important benefit to it conferred by
Section 73(8-b).
As noted above, [the employee] joining the [second agency] did not change the fact that
she was a former employee [of the first agency] who was prohibited by the post-employment
restrictions from contracting with [that agency]. In [that agency]’s submission to the
Commission, the head of the agency certified, as required by Section 73(8-b), that the former
employee has “expertise, knowledge or experience with respect to a particular matter which
meets the needs of the agency and is otherwise unavailable at a comparable cost.” This
certification effectively eliminates the need to apply Section 73(4)(a) to the situation because it
establishes that competitive bidding would not generate a better option. Notably, the statute
grants authority to seek such relief to the agency itself; the former employee cannot apply. This
certification, with the Commission’s oversight, helps to ensure that there is no appearance of
undue influence or favorable treatment. Section 73(4) is designed to address a concern that is not
present here.
CONCLUSION
Under the circumstances presented, Section 73(8-b) applies and both satisfies and
outweighs Section 73(4)(a). This result preserves the option for [the first agency] to contract with
its former employee, with the acquiescence of the current employing agency, while alleviating
the conflict-of-interest concerns addressed in Section 73(4)(a).

Advisory Opinion No. 25-01: The confidentiality afforded guidance and
guidance-related communications by Executive
Law § 94(7)(b) may be deemed waived by the
misleading, inaccurate, or incomplete public
disclosure of the nature or substance of the guidance
and related communications by the recipient. In
such instances, the Commission or Commission
staff may release information relating to the
guidance request, including but not limited to an
unredacted version of the request for guidance and
of any guidance provided and any related
communications between the requester and the
Commission.
QUESTION
Does Executive Law § 94(7)(b) preclude the Commission or Commission staff from
publicly correcting a public disclosure or utterance concerning the nature or substance of guidance
requested from or provided by the Commission, and of communications related to such guidance,
that is misleadingly, inaccurate or materially incomplete?
ANSWER
Requests by individuals to the Commission or Commission staff for guidance and the
guidance provided to individuals in response to such requests, as well as communications between
the requester and the Commission related to such guidance, are generally deemed confidential by
operation of statute, and in most circumstances, the Commission is obligated to respect that
confidentiality. However, in addition to its statutory obligation to provide advice and guidance to
individual state officers and employees and others subject to its jurisdiction upon their request, the
Commission is also statutorily obligated to provide advice and guidance and to educate and inform
all of those subject to its jurisdiction, as well as the public at large, with respect to the requirements

2
and prohibitions of the state’s ethics and lobbying laws and regulations and to ensure compliance
with those law and regulations. Particularly as the mandate for universal annual workforce ethics
training has produced a heightened sensitivity to, and a markedly increased volume of requests for,
governmental ethics advice and guidance, the broad latter obligation requires, and common law
principles of individual waiver provide, that the Commission and Commission staff be able
publicly to correct public misstatements or erroneous characterizations by those seeking guidance
from the Commission of their request for guidance, the guidance they received from the
Commission and any related communications with the Commission when necessary to prevent the
dissemination of incorrect or misleading information concerning the requirements and prohibitions
of the state’s ethics and lobbying laws and regulations and the Commission’s administration of
those laws and regulations.
Discussion
The Commission’s governing statute, Executive Law § 94, at subdivision 7(a), charges the
Commission with a broad obligation to provide ethics and lobbying guidance, through a dedicated
staff unit, to “all persons whose conduct it oversees,” other than members and employees of the
Legislature, as follows:
7. Advice and guidance. (a) The commission shall establish a unit or units solely for
ethics and lobbying guidance, and give such prompt, informal advice to persons
whose conduct it oversees, except with respect to members of the legislature and
legislative staff, who shall seek advice from the legislative ethics commission in the
first instance.
(See also id., § 94(6)(c)(i).) The statute encourages guidance-seeking from Commission staff by
granting conditional protective effect to staff-rendered guidance1 and confidentiality to the
guidance recipient’s communications with the Commission:
(b) Persons receiving such informal advice may rely on that advice absent
misrepresentation or omission of material facts to the commission and such
communications with the commission shall be treated as confidential, except as disclosure
1 The Commission can also render guidance of general applicability through formal advisory opinions, either upon
written request or, as here, on its own initiative:
(c) The commission may also render, on written request or on its own initiative, advisory opinions, and may
allow for public comment before issuance of an advisory opinion. Such an opinion rendered by the
commission shall be relied on by those subject to the commission's jurisdiction and until, or unless, amended,
superseded, or revoked. Such opinion may also be relied upon by any such person, and may be introduced
and shall be a defense, in any criminal or civil action.
Executive Law § 94(7)(c). Commission practice has been to treat requests for such formal guidance and related
communications between the requester and the Commission as clothed with the same confidentiality as requests for
informal guidance.

3
is needed to prevent or rectify a crime or fraud, or prevent a substantial threat to public
health or safety or if required by court order.
In addition to providing advice and guidance generally, the Commission has adopted formal
regulations that prescribe procedures for the approval of certain external activities that are
governed by the ethics laws, specifically, the receipt of honoraria, see 19 NYCRR Part 930; official
activity expense and service payments and reimbursement, see 9 NYCRR Part 931; outside
activities, see 19 NYCRR Part 932; and attendance at widely attended events – 19 NYCRR Part
933. With the exception of statewide elected officials and agency heads, for whom the
Commission is the sole “approving authority,” approval for these external activities must be sought
and obtained from, or (with respect to attendance at widely attended events and engaging in certain
outside activities) notice given to, the head of the applicant’s agency or to his or her designee
before any application, where one is required, can be made to the Commission’s Advice and
Guidance Unit. (See 19 NYCRR § 930.2(a) and 930.4; id., §931.2(a) and 931.3; id., § 933.2(a),
932.5 and 932.6; and id., § 933.4(a)(7)(ii).)
Although, except for requests by state-wide elected officials and agency heads, agency-
level approval must be obtained before the Commission, if its approval is also required, can
consider a request, such agency-level approvals and the related communications between state
officers and employees and their agency approving authorities are not shielded by the
confidentiality provision in Executive Law §94(7)(b) and have no protective effect for the
requester. In other words, with comparatively small2 exception, most guidance requested and given
is neither statutorily confidential nor insulating. However anomalous this may seem, the absence
of confidentiality for agency-rendered guidance and communications has never been challenged
and has never been found to be a deterrent to guidance seeking or an obstacle the legislative
objective embodied in Executive Law §94(7). Nor has the conditional nature of the protection
afforded by advice rendered under Executive Law §94(7)(a) been considered inhibiting.
Waiver. Under normal concepts of preservation and waiver, even with respect to statutorily
privileged matter, protection for confidential information is deemed relinquished when the
holder of the privilege manifests an intention inconsistent with the preservation of
confidentiality, whether by conduct inconsistent with preservation, or explicitly:
“Waiver is a voluntary and intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known
existing right or privilege, which, except for such waiver, would have been enjoyed.
. . . It may be expressed formally or it may be implied as a necessary consequence
of the waiver's conduct inconsistent with an assertion of retention of the right.”
Livera v. First Nat'l State Bank, 535 F. Supp. 1063, 1065 (EDNY 1982), quoting
from Buffum v. Chase Nat'l Bank of New York, 192 F.2d 58, 60-61 (7th Cir. 1951),
cert. denied, 342 U.S. 944 (1952).
2 That is not to say that the volume is not in absolute terms substantial: in 2024 alone, the Advice and Guidance Unit
responded to more than 1,300 guidance requests, including rendering 377 written informal letter opinions, an
increase of more than fifty percent over the previous year. While some of these requests were from officials for
whom the Commission is the approving authority, the overwhelming number were from, or made by agency ethics
officers or counsel, on behalf of individuals who were first required to obtain approval from their employing
agencies.

4
As has been stated with respect to the waiver of confidential attorney-client
communications:
The privilege is waived when the circumstances surrounding the disclosure evidence
a lack of intent to protect the confidentiality of the privileged communications. The
Master found that, as a matter of fact, the selective, intentional or negligent, release
of various privileged communications constitutes a waiver. While an isolated
inadvertent disclosure dies not waive the privilege, Mendenhall v. Barber, 531 F.
Supp. 951, 954 (N.D. Ill. 1982), one need not prove an intent to waive for a waiver
to occur. In re Grand Jury Investigation of Ocean Transportation, 604 F.2d 672 (D.C.
Ct. Appeals 1979), cert denied, 444 U.S. 915 (1979); Women in City Gov't United v.
City of N.Y., No. 75 Civ. 2868 (MJL), 1986 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 26669, at *5 (S.D.N.Y.
Apr. 16, 1986).
The Appellate Division, Second Department, has stated the general principle as follows:
"A valid waiver requires no more than the voluntary and intentional abandonment of
a known right which, but for the waiver would have been enforceable" (Golfo v Kycia
Assoc., Inc., 45 AD3d 531, 532 (2d Dep’t 2007) [internal quotation marks
omitted]; also see Fundamental Portfolio Advisors, Inc. v Tocqueville Asset Mgt.,
L.P., 7 NY3d 96, 104 (2006).
Mercado v. Schwartz, 209 A.D.3d 30, 40 (2d Dep’t 2022) (waiver of claimed contractual right to
depose plaintiff’s expert witness by counsel’s assent to contrary pretrial order); cf. People v.
Jenkins, 66 A.D.3d 800, (2nd Dep’t 2009) (suppression motion properly denied; “voluntarily and
intentionally discarding” items was an act that constituted “a waiver of any legitimate expectation
of privacy,” citing People v. Ramirez-Portoreal, 88 N.Y.2d 99, 110 (1996)). Nor may a party “assert
the privilege over a communication and then later make partial self-serving disclosures of the
allegedly privileged material.” Hussain v. Burton & Doyle of Great Neck, LLC, No. 14-CV-5924
(SIL), 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 144223, at *13 (EDNY. Oct. 18, 2016) (claimed confidentiality of
trust agreement waived by, inter alia, defendant’s references to and reliance upon portions of it in
their motion for summary judgment), citing In re Cty. of Erie, 473 F.3d 413, 419 (2d Cir.
2007); Crawford v. Coram Fire Dist., No. 12-CV 3850, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 59582, 2014 WL
168203, at 3 (EDNY 2014); Pall Corp. v. Cuno Inc., 268 F.R.D. 167, 168 (E.D.N.Y. 2010) (a
party's partial disclosure of and/or affirmative reliance upon privileged communications places
those communications at issue, likely defeating any claim of attorney-client privilege over them).
See generally Westmoreland v. CBS, Inc., 97 F.R.D. 703, 706 (SDNY 1983) (in defamation action,
defendant cannot hold out internal report as “substantiating its accusations and, when challenged,
decline to reveal the Report contending that it is a confidential internal study utilized solely for
self-evaluation and self-improvement”).
With respect to the attributes of preservation and waiver, there is nothing that materially
distinguishes the confidentiality conferred by Executive Law § 94(7)(b) from the statutory,
common law and contractual confidentiality discussed above. That that provision is silent with

5
respect to waiver does not preclude the application of well-settled common-law precepts; on the
contrary, in the absence of an explicit proscription in a statute, it is generally assumed that such
precepts are intended to apply. See generally Mayorga v. Tate, 302 A.D.2d 11, 17-18, 752 N.Y.S.2d
353, 358 (App. Div. 2nd Dept. 2002) (the absence of waiver formalities in CPLR 4504, in contrast
to predecessor CPA provision, indicates that "’as is the case of the attorney-client
privilege, waiver [of the physician-patient privilege] may, under the cases, be implied'" (emphasis
supplied), quoting Lynch v Mutual Life Ins. Co. of N.Y., 55 Misc 2d 179, 181, 284 N.Y.S.2d 768
(Su. Ct. 1967), quoting Second Preliminary Report of the Advisory Committee on Practice and
Procedure [1958, at 92]); Oden v. Chemung County Indus. Dev. Agency, 87 N.Y.2d 81, 86 (1995)
(statutes in derogation of common law to be narrowly construed). Cf. Kelly v. N.Y. State Ethics
Comm'n, 161 Misc. 2d 706, 716, 614 N.Y.S.2d 996, 1002 (Sup. Ct. 1994)(State Ethics
Commission’s determination that petitioner had violated Public Officers Law § 74(3)(d) and (h)
based upon facts disclosed in his request for guidance under Public Officers Law § 73(8) and
without the issuance of a 15-day notice of allegations and an opportunity to respond “was not
arbitrary and capricious, was not made in violation of lawful procedure, and was not affected by
an error of law.”) A recipient of Commission guidance who inaccurately or incompletely discloses
that guidance publicly stands on no better footing than those who deliberately reveal other initially
protected communications for strategic or other advantaging reasons. Having done so, they cannot
be heard to complain if the Commission responds by correcting and completing the record.
Such corrective responses are warranted because even in the context of an individual
guidance matter, misleading, inaccurate or incomplete public mischaracterizations of the advice
sought from the Commission and rendered by it can have broad detrimental consequences, not
only for the Commission in performing its statutorily mandated work, but for the hundreds of
thousands of individuals who are within its jurisdiction and whose conduct is subject to the duties
and obligations of the state’s ethics and lobbying laws. Under the Ethics Commission Reform Act,
L.2022, ch. 56, Part QQ, the Commission is charged with administering triennial ethics training
triennially to lobbyists and lobbyists clients and annually to the entire state executive branch
workforce. The propagation of misleading and inaccurate mischaracterizations of Commission
guidance, if left unrectified, can undermine the enormous effort to educate the state workforce and
the regulated lobbying community. That alone, as well as the need to ensure accurate
representations of Commission guidance, amply justifies the Commission in taking corrective
action.
CONCLUSION
Accordingly, and for the above reasons, the confidentiality afforded advice-related
communications by Executive Law § 94(7)(b) may be deemed waived by the misleading,
inaccurate or incomplete public disclosure by the requesting person of the nature or substance of
the request made, the guidance rendered or guidance-related communications with the
Commission. In such instances, the Commission may release or otherwise provide information
relating to the guidance request, including but not limited to an unredacted version of the request
for guidance and any associated communications and of any guidance provided.

Advisory Opinion No. 24-03: Application of Public Officers Law § 74 to
employees of a State agency who have
formed a not-for-profit corporate entity
whose purpose is to solicit and accept
private sector contributions of gifts to the
agency in support of the agency’s mission.
INTRODUCTION
The following advisory opinion is issued by the New York State Commission on Ethics
and Lobbying in Government (the “Commission”), pursuant to Executive Law § 94(7)(c), in
response to an inquiry from the Ethics Officer at the New York State Department of Environmental
Conservation (the “Department”). Two employees of the Department had founded a not-for-profit
corporate entity called The Forest Ranger Foundation, Inc. (the “Foundation”), and had made
requests to the Department for approval to serve as officers of the Foundation. The purpose of the
Foundation includes collecting donations of “funding to provide innovative and cutting-edge
technology, equipment, supports, and services for Forest Rangers . . . that may otherwise be
unavailable or inaccessible due to limited funding and/or process restrictions . . . ”1 Forest Rangers
are employees of the Department.
The two employees are not policymakers, so their requests for approval of the outside
activity fell under the discretion of the Department as the employing agency.2 Given the novelty
of the situation, the Department’s Ethics Officer requested an informal opinion from Commission
staff as to whether the requests for approval of the outside activities could be granted, as well as
whether, and how, the Foundation could make donations to the Department. However, as this is a
matter of first impression, and there is no existing Commission precedent directly on point, the
Commission is releasing this formal Advisory Opinion holding that, absent explicit authorization
1 Fourth Clause, Certificate of Incorporation.
2 See Title 19 NYCRR Part 932.5. The approval process outlined in the outside activity regulations apply only to
policymakers, many of whose outside activities are subject to further review by the Commission. The outside
activities of non-policymakers are subject to review pursuant to the policies and procedures of the employing
agency.

2
from the agency to do so, Public Officers Law § 74(3)(d) and (h) prohibit State employees from
engaging in organized efforts to solicit and accept gifts to their employing agency. While the
motives of the employees in question appear to be commendable, permitting such activities will
reasonably create an impression among the public that the employees, or the agency, are engaged
in an artful tactic to benefit themselves. There is no provision in the law that permits State
employees, on their own initiative, to directly solicit or accept gifts on behalf of their employing
agency. The establishment and operation of the Foundation also interferes with the Department’s
normal governance and decision-making processes as the Foundation will constitute a separate
decision-making body aimed at affecting operations of the Department.
BACKGROUND
The Department’s Ethics Officer contacted Commission staff with an inquiry about two
applications the agency had received for outside activity approval. Two of the Department’s
employees had founded a not-for-profit entity – the Foundation – without prior notice to the
Department, and now sought approval from the Department to sit on the Foundation’s Board of
Directors.
Pursuant to its Certificate of Incorporation, the Corporation’s mission statement is as
follows:
The Corporation is formed for the purpose of lessening the burdens of government
by fostering, encouraging, and promoting private sector support for the New York
State Forest Rangers and providing such support to and for the New York State
Forest Rangers and its governmental purposes as part of the Division of Forest
Protection of the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.3
The following specific purposes are listed in the Certificate of Incorporation:
(1) Secure funding to provide innovative and cutting-edge technology, equipment,
supports, and services for Forest Rangers in furtherance of such purposes that
may otherwise be unavailable or inaccessible due to limited government
funding and/or process restrictions;
(2) Ensure Forest Rangers have access to the highest quality education and training
possible in order to assure their safety and ability to provide public safety and
state land protection through expertise in wildland search, rescue, fire, law
enforcement, and incident management throughout the State of New York;
(3) Conduct any and all lawful activities which may be necessary or useful in
furtherance of these stated purposes.4
In furtherance of such purposes, the Corporation may expend, contribute, disburse,
and otherwise dispose of its funds, income and other property by making grants and
contributions to, and cooperating with and otherwise voluntarily financially
assisting directly or indirectly such persons, any government entity including, but
not limited to, the Division of Forest Protection of the New York State Department
3 Fourth Clause, Certificate of Incorporation.
4 See, Id.(emphasis supplied).

3
of Environmental Conservation . . .5
The Foundation is governed by a Board of Directors of up to nine directors, all of whom
must be “currently employed by the Division of Forest Protection of the New York State
Department of Environmental Conservation as an entry-level Forest Ranger.”6 Directors earn no
salary or compensation other than entitlement to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses,7 and
the Foundation is not to be used “for the pecuniary profit or financial gain of its directors or
officers.”8 The Foundation, and the participation of individual Forest Rangers with the Foundation,
have not been formally endorsed or sanctioned by the Department.
APPLICABLE LAW
Public Officers Law § 74 sets forth the State Code of Ethics, which is intended to prevent
State officers and employees from engaging in conduct that present actual or apparent conflicts of
interest. Section 74(2) states the general rule: “No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should
have any interest, financial or otherwise, direct or indirect, or engage in any business or transaction
or professional activity or incur any obligation of any nature, which is in substantial conflict with
the proper discharge of his duties in the public interest.”
The Code of Conduct, in Subdivision 3 of Public Officers Law § 74, sets forth minimum
standards of conduct. Conduct that falls short of any of these standards presents a conflict of
interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest. The standards of conduct relevant to the present
inquiry include the following:
d. No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should use or attempt to use his official
position to secure unwarranted privileges or exemptions for himself or others.
h. An officer or employee of a state agency . . . should endeavor to pursue a course of
conduct which will not raise suspicion among the public that he or she is likely to be engaged in
acts that are in violation of his or her trust.
The gift restrictions are set forth in Public Officers Law § 73(5):
5. No . . . state officer or employee . . . shall, directly or indirectly:
(a) solicit, accept or receive any gift having more than a nominal value, whether in
the form of money, service, loan, travel, lodging, meals, refreshments,
entertainment, discount, forbearance or promise, or in any other form, under
circumstances in which it could reasonably be inferred that the gift was intended to
influence him or her, or could reasonably be expected to influence him or her, in
the performance of his or her official duties or was intended as a reward for any
official action on his or her part. No person shall, directly or indirectly, offer or
make any such gift to a statewide elected official, or any state officer or employee,
5 Id.
6 Bylaws I.3.
7 Bylaws I.8.
8 Fourth Clause, Certificate of Incorporation.

4
member of the legislature or legislative employee under such circumstances.
(b) solicit, accept or receive any gift, as defined in section one-c of the legislative
law, from any person who is prohibited from delivering such gift pursuant to section
one-m of the legislative law unless under the circumstances it is not reasonable to
infer that the gift was intended to influence him or her; or
(c) permit the solicitation, acceptance, or receipt of any gift, as defined in section
one-c of the legislative law, from any person who is prohibited from delivering such
gift pursuant to section one-m of the legislative law to a third party including a
charitable organization, on such official's designation or recommendation or on his
or her behalf, under circumstances where it is reasonable to infer that the gift was
intended to influence him or her.
DISCUSSION
The key question presented is whether it is permissible for State employees, on their own
initiative, to create and sit on the board of a not-for-profit corporation whose purpose is to solicit
and accept gifts for their employing agency. The Commission has noted that it “conceives of few,
if any, circumstances in which the solicitation by a State officer or employee in his or her official
capacity of a personal gift of any value would be appropriate behavior or be authorized by the
provisions of Public Officers Law § 74.”9 A more difficult question arises when individual State
employees undertake efforts to solicit gifts for the ostensibly public purpose of supporting their
own employing agency. The Commission finds that such activity, while commendable on its face,
blurs the line between state and private interests, can give rise to confusion among the public, and
creates an appearance of a conflict of interest that violates Public Officers Law § 74.
The Department’s Commissioner is authorized by statute to “acquire real or personal
property, including acquisition by condemnation, appropriation, gift, grant, devise or bequest.”10
In Advisory Opinion No. 95-38, the State Ethics Commission held that the Department could
accept donations directly from individuals and businesses, but with important caveats:
The Commission concludes that DEC may accept donations from individuals,
businesses or organizations whose activities are subject to its jurisdiction. However,
it may not accept donations from individuals or entities under investigation by or
in litigation with the agency. Decisions as to the propriety of a donation must be
made by the Commissioner on a case-by-case basis, considering its source, timing
and amount. . .. DEC may not accept donations where the equipment or money
donated is conditioned upon its use in a particular geographic region.11
Moreover, the agency could not accept any donation that is conditioned upon its use in a
specific geographic region:
9 Advisory Opinion No. 94-16, p. 6 (italic added).
10 N.Y. Environmental Conservation Law § 3-0301(2)(l). There is no statutory provision permitting employees of
the Department independently to receive gifts for the Department.
11 Advisory Opinion No. 95-38, p. 6.

5
The Commission concludes that donations made to DEC must be available for
agency use as the Commissioner deems appropriate. To hold otherwise would
unduly restrict the Commissioner in applying agency resources as circumstances
require, and could result in those employed in certain DEC regions enjoying better
working conditions or having better equipment than those employed elsewhere. A
donor cannot, in essence, make a donation to DEC in exchange for better services
in its area. The Commissioner must be free to determine the allocation of the
agency's resources statewide based upon his or her best judgment.12
These restrictions leave no room for lower-level employees to act as intermediaries,
shielding donors and their gifts from scrutiny by the Commissioner. This additional layer interferes
with the Commissioner’s obligation to consider each donation on a case-by-case basis, and leaves
open the possibility that improper donations will be received, whether from ineligible donors or
others. Moreover, as the Foundation is specifically dedicated to supporting the Forest Rangers and
the Department’s Division of Forest Protection, its offers to the Department come with strings
attached that preclude their acceptance by the Department.
Additionally, the Department’s employees who serve on the board of the Foundation or as
its officers will both practically and legally have conflicting loyalties to the Department and the
public, on the one hand, and, on the other, to the Foundation, to which they will owe fiduciary
responsibilities. Although the employees are seeking, among other things, to improve the
Department’s capabilities and the working conditions of its employees (that is, themselves), that
is not to say that the interests of the Foundation are co-extensive with the interests of the
Department. To the contrary, it is inevitable that the interests of the Foundation, and consequently,
the interests of its officers and directors, will conflict, as the Foundation is directed, as defined by
its certificate of incorporation, to merely one aspect of the Department’s operations, while the
Department must balance and prioritize among all of its statewide responsibilities. The dual and
conflicting loyalties created are in contravention of Public Officers Law § 74.13
Finally, the activities of the Foundation are apt to give rise to confusion amongst the public
about its operations. Is the Foundation the same as or related to the Department? Does the
Foundation represent the Department? Why is the Department seeking donations? Why is the
Department using an independent entity to solicit donations? Are Department employees seeking
donations as state officers and employees of the Department or as agents of the Foundation? At
what point, if any, will the propriety of donations made to the Foundation, especially from donors
who have business before the Department, be assessed, and by whom? What authority does the
Foundation have with respect to the Department? What happens to donations that are declined by
the Department? The independent actions of the employees, which are not coordinated with the
Department, can create the impression that the employees are acting in pursuit of their own
interests, or the interests of the Foundation, rather than the best interests of the Department.
12 Id.
13 Advisory Opinion No. 99-04, p. 3.

6
CONCLUSION
Public Officers Law § 74(3)(d) and (h) prohibit the DEC employees from forming and
sitting on the board of a corporate entity whose mission is to receive or solicit public contributions
of money or equipment to benefit their employing agency. Any organized effort by agency
employees to solicit and/or receive donations to their employing agency must be explicitly
approved by their agency, and the solicitation efforts must clearly state (i) that the solicitation is
endorsed by the agency; (ii) the intended use of the contributions, (iii) an explanation of the
decision to seek these items or funds by donation, and (iv) that the agency will return any
contribution that, in its judgment, is improper. Further, the agency must consider each donation on
a case-by-case basis as set forth in Advisory Opinion No. 95-38.

Advisory Opinion No. 24-02: Application of Public Officers Law § 74 to a
member of a State Board who also serves as
“of counsel” to a law firm that represents
clients before the State Board.
INTRODUCTION
The following advisory opinion is issued by the New York State Commission on Ethics
and Lobbying in Government (“Commission”), pursuant to Executive Law § 94(7)(c), in response
to an inquiry from Mr. Doe, the Chair of the [ ] Board of Directors (the “State Board”).
The inquiry concerns the application of Public Officers Law § 74, the State Code of Ethics, to Mr.
Doe’s relationship with a private law firm where he currently serves as [ ] Partner but will
soon transition to “of counsel” status. The law firm represents clients with matters before the State
Board, and Mr. Doe currently recuses himself when a matter involving the law firm comes before
him in his capacity as Chair of the State Board.
In an inquiry to Commission staff, Mr. Doe asked whether, after his transition to “of
counsel” status at the law firm, he must continue to recuse himself in his State Board capacity from
matters in which an interested party is represented by his law firm. Commission staff issued
guidance, in the form of an informal advisory opinion, opining that Mr. Doe should continue to
recuse himself in his State Board capacity from matters in which the law firm is directly involved,
even after his status at the law firm changes from [ ] Partner to “of counsel.” Pursuant to the
Commission’s Resolution 23-02, the Commissioners reviewed this guidance before its release to
Mr. Doe, who subsequently requested the Commission’s formal review of his inquiry. The
Commission now concludes that the State official cannot, in his capacity as Chair (or Member) of
the State Board, participate in any matter in which the law firm is involved, regardless of whether
the State official serves the law firm as [ ] Partner or “of counsel,” or in some other capacity.
Recusal is clearly the proper remedy under the circumstances presented.
Restoring public trust in state government

2
BACKGROUND
Mr. Doe was recently appointed by the Governor to serve as Chair of the State Board. In
this statutory, uncompensated role, the Chair presides over meetings and submits
recommendations and information concerning the business, duties, and affairs of the agency.1 The
Chair also serves as an ex-officio member of all standing committees, including the Audit
Committee, Governance Committee, and Finance & Program Committees, and serves as the Chair
of those committees.2 Further, the Chair serves as Chair of the Board of Directors for the state
agency’s subsidiaries. As Chair, he may delegate to employees or officers of the agency any such
duties or responsibilities as deemed appropriate.3
Outside of his role as Chair of the State Board, Mr. Doe serves as [ ] Partner of a law
firm whose practice concentrates on the areas of affordable housing and community development
transactions using various tax incentives, including Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, New
Markets Tax Credits and Historic Tax Credits. As [ ] Partner, Mr. Doe serves as an
administrator for the firm and does not represent any clients personally. As a [ ] Partner, he
receives compensation based upon the firm’s overall revenue. Mr. Doe plans to retire and resign
from his membership in the firm, transitioning to “of counsel” status. In this capacity, he will
provide services to clients outside of New York, and his compensation will be limited to work for
the firm’s out-of-state clients, rather than the firm’s general revenue.
The law firm represents clients that have matters before the State Board and its subsidiaries.
Since joining the State Board, Mr. Doe has recused himself from any matter involving the law firm
that would otherwise come before him in his State Board capacity. According to Mr. Doe, the law
firm has developed a process for identifying potential matters that may come before the State
Board and its subsidiaries, but he also noted that this process is time-consuming and requires
additional resources, the cost of which is absorbed by the firm. Mr. Doe further advises that in his
“of counsel” role, he will no longer have access to client reports, which will create a challenge to
identifying matters for recusal. Mr. Doe also suggests that a continuing recusal obligation could
create difficulty for the State Board meeting quorum requirements and there would be matters up
for approval that would not be approved were he to recuse himself. Mr. Doe argues that upon
taking “of counsel” status, it should no longer be necessary to recuse himself in his State Board
capacity from matters involving the law firm.
APPLICABLE LAW
Public Officers Law § 74 sets forth the State Code of Ethics, which is intended to prevent
State officers and employees from engaging in conduct that present actual or apparent conflicts of
interest. Section 74(2) states the general rule: “No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should
have any interest, financial or otherwise, direct or indirect, or engage in any business or transaction
or professional activity or incur any obligation of any nature, which is in substantial conflict with
the proper discharge of his duties in the public interest.”
1 Section 2, Article II, NYS Housing Finance Agency By-laws (as amended September 10, 2015).
2 Section 1, Article VII, NYS Housing Finance Agency By-laws (as amended September 10, 2015).
3 Section 2, Article II, NYS Housing Finance Agency By-laws (as amended September 10, 2015).

3
The Code of Conduct, in Subdivision 3 of Public Officers Law § 74, sets forth minimum
standards of conduct. Conduct that falls short of any of these standards presents a conflict of
interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest. The standards of conduct relevant to the present
inquiry include the following:
d. No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should use or attempt to use his official
position to secure unwarranted privileges or exemptions for himself or others.
e. No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should engage in any transaction as
representative or agent of the state with any business entity in which he has a direct or indirect
financial interest that might reasonably tend to conflict with the proper discharge of his official
duties.
f. An officer or employee of a state agency . . . should not by his conduct give reasonable
basis for the impression that any person can improperly influence him or unduly enjoy his favor
in the performance of his official duties, or that he is affected by the kinship, rank, position or
influence of any party or person.
h. An officer or employee of a state agency . . . should endeavor to pursue a course of
conduct which will not raise suspicion among the public that he is likely to be engaged in acts that
are in violation of his trust.
DISCUSSION
The Code of Ethics is intended to prevent State officers and employees from engaging in
conduct that presents a conflict of interest, or the appearance of a conflict, with their State position.
Further, the law is intended to promote the public's trust and confidence in government through
the prevention of favoritism, undue influence, corruption, and abuses of official position.4
Commission precedent clearly contemplates recusal as the proper remedy when a State
official is called upon to act on a matter that implicates the official’s private interests. In Advisory
Opinion No. 01-02, for example, the State Ethics Commission held that the President of a SUNY
campus could continue to serve on a board of directors of a for-profit computer hardware company
that was doing business with SUNY, provided that the SUNY President recused herself in both
capacities from discussions or decisions concerning the other. Significantly, recusal was held to
be appropriate even though it was noted that the actual conflict presented was minimal, given that
SUNY’s procurement process was largely isolated from the purview of the President.
More directly on point, in Advisory Opinion No. 93-17, an attorney in private practice,
who also served on a State Appeals Board, asked whether representatives of his law firm could
represent parties appearing before the Appeals Board. The State Ethics Commission noted that the
law firm and its members and employees were not subject to the Public Officers Law and therefore
were not themselves prohibited from appearing before the Appeals Board on behalf of the
interested parties. However, it also stated, in no uncertain terms, that the attorney must recuse
himself from matters in which his law firm was involved:
4 Advisory Opinion No. 95-18.

4
It would be a clear conflict of interest were the Board member to participate to any
degree on a matter before the Board in which a member or associate of his firm
represented a party. Even disclosing his relationship to his colleagues, to all parties and
the Board would not cure the nearly inevitable suspicion that the Board member could,
in so participating, be acting in violation of his trust. Consequently, in such instances,
he should recuse himself from participation in any Board proceeding which involves
his law firm. Furthermore, he must not communicate with the firm's lawyers concerning
the matter before the Board or share in the net revenues generated from such
appearances.5
The text of Advisory Opinion No. 93-17 does not specify the attorney’s status with the law
firm, but the Commission assumes he was an equity partner in light of the reference to the “net
revenues” rule in the above excerpt, which would apply to a member of a law firm but not to an
associate or “of counsel.”6 Here, Mr. Doe suggests that the need to recuse is diminished because,
while holding “of counsel” status, he will not be in a position to directly benefit from matters
before the State Board since his compensation will be solely from clients outside of New York,
and not from the firm’s overall revenue. However, preventing an explicit potential for personal
benefit is not the sole purpose of the ethics laws. As stated in Advisory Opinion No. 93-17:
[A] public official must not only be innocent of any wrongdoing, but he must be alert
at all times so that his acts and conduct give the public no cause for suspicion. He must
give no appearance of a potential conflict between his official duties and personal
activities even though an actual conflict is not present.7
The Commission rejects the suggestion that Mr. Doe’s change in status from [ ] Partner
to “of counsel” should, by itself, have any immediate effect on Mr. Doe’s continuing obligation to
recuse from matters before the State Board in which the law firm in involved.
Moreover, under established Commission precedent, Mr. Doe would almost certainly have
to continue to recuse himself from matters involving the law firm for a period of time even if he
severed his relationship with the law firm entirely. In Advisory Opinion No. 94-11, the
Commission developed the “reverse two-year bar” to address potential conflicts of interest (or the
appearance of such conflicts) when a person enters unpaid, policymaking State service from the
private sector. The Opinion adopted a presumption that an unpaid member of a State board must
be recused from involvement in a matter that involves a former employer or business that he or
she left within the last two years. While in some instances this presumption can be overcome
though a factor-based analysis,8 none of the factors is relevant here because Mr. Doe still has a
5 Advisory Opinion No. 93-17, p. 5.
6 See Public Officers Law § 73(10).
7 Advisory Opinion No. 93-17, p. 4, citing, 1979 Op. Atty. Gen. 66.
8 The presumption requiring recusal could be rebutted by looking at certain factors, including but not limited to:
• Whether the board member was in an employment relationship with the applicant, which implies
daily oversight and control, or was in a consulting relationship, which suggests a more temporary
connection;
• Whether the board member was an officer or senior official of the applicant;
• Whether the board member or the applicant had a fiduciary relationship with the other;
• Whether the applicant is the actual former employer or business entity with which the board member

5
continuing business relationship with the law firm, only strengthening his recusal obligation.9
The Commission notes Mr. Doe’s averment that the recusal obligation is an administrative
burden and expense for the law firm, but it should not be beyond the ability of the State Board to
track matters in which a party is represented by Mr. Doe’s law firm. At the very least, Mr. Doe is
obligated to recuse himself from any matter at the earliest opportunity upon learning that his law
firm is involved in the matter.
Finally, a speculative, future need for the State Board to meet quorum requirements is not
a legitimate consideration when determining proper application of the ethics rules.
The Commission also takes this opportunity to clarify that recusal in this type of situation
means disclosure of the conflict; abstaining from all discussion regarding the matter, whether
formal or informal; leaving the room during deliberation and votes; and declining to vote on such
matters.
CONCLUSION
The Commission hereby concludes that Public Officers Law § 74 requires Mr. Doe to
continue to recuse himself, in his capacity as Chair of the State Board, from any matter involving
the law firm that comes before the State Board, whether he is a member of the law firm, its [ ]
Partner, “of counsel,” or he has some other business relationship with the law firm.

subsequent proceeding concerning the person who requested it and who acted in good faith, unless
material facts were omitted or misstated by the person in the request for opinion or related
supporting documentation.

FREDERICK A. DAVIE SANFORD N. BERLAND
